title: Solidarity
hookLine: in Poland, striking workers kneel for Mass at the shipyard gate, and faith and a trade union help bring peaceful change

cards: The gate of a shipyard in Gdańsk, on the Polish coast, is covered in flowers. Someone has hung a picture of the pope on it, and a wooden cross. Inside, the workers are on strike.

Outside, a priest sets up an altar, and the strikers kneel on the concrete for Mass. Others line up for confession on folding chairs by the fence. The government is communist, wary of the church, and watching.
The workers want a union of their own, free of the party, and they paint its name on their banners.

teach.b: The union was called Solidarność, Solidarity, and an electrician named Lech Wałęsa became its face. It was a trade union, not a church, and its members included believers and nonbelievers.
But in Poland the Catholic Church was a large institution the state didn't control, and the two leaned on each other. The pope was Polish: John Paul the Second.
At the start of his time as pope, he told the crowds, in effect, do not be afraid. Jesus says it in the Gospels.
When the disciples see him walking on the water, terrified, the King James Bible has him say: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid."
Before the strikes, when the pope came home to Poland, crowds gathered in the open for his Masses. Then the crackdown came. Martial law.
In Warsaw a young priest, Jerzy Popiełuszko, said Masses for the homeland, packed with workers, and kept repeating Paul's line to the Romans: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
Secret police officers abducted and killed him. His grave became a place of pilgrimage. And still the movement didn't turn to violence.

teach.h: A ROUND TABLE, NOT A WAR.
teach.b: Years later, the government sat down at a round table with Solidarity and agreed to partly free elections, and Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to contest.
Solidarity is also a word in Christian teaching: people are bound up with one another, so another's burden is partly yours. Paul says it plainly: "Bear ye one another's burdens."

how: In Catholic teaching, solidarity is one of the principles of social teaching, and Catholics pray for workers on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker. Catholics honor Jerzy Popiełuszko as a martyr, and his grave in Warsaw is visited by pilgrims.

games.q: you're a striking worker inside the shipyard. a priest is setting up an altar at the gate. what do you do?
o: stay on the picket line and ignore it.
kneel on the concrete for Mass.
go home before the police come.
games.why: strikers knelt for Mass at the gate and lined up for confession by the fence, while the state watched.

practice: Start with what's around you, the chair, the light, your clothes, your next meal: somebody built, wired, sewed, grew, drove or cleaned for each.

Picture a few of those workers, a night shift, a warehouse, a field, a shipyard, and let one of their burdens sit with you a moment. If you pray, pray for workers by name or by trade; if you don't, let the thanks be enough.

wordCard.voice: Solidarity. The Polish trade union that grew alongside the church and helped bring peaceful change. And an old idea: your neighbor's burden is partly yours.

carryVoice: Your line: be not afraid. In the end, a round table, not a war. Until tomorrow.
